claim: The RAP imaging modality uses a novel design inspired by a Newtonian telescope to image multiple spatially separated samples without moving parts or robotics.
source: We introduce a random-access parallel (RAP) imaging modality that uses a novel design inspired by a Newtonian telescope to image multiple spatially separated samples without moving parts or robotics.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the system design.

claim: The RAP system enables near-simultaneous image capture of multiple petri dishes.
source: This scheme enables near-simultaneous image capture of multiple petri dishes and random-access imaging with sub-millisecond switching times at the full resolution of the camera.
evidence: This capability is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in the results section.

claim: The RAP system has sub-millisecond switching times at the full resolution of the camera.
source: This scheme enables near-simultaneous image capture of multiple petri dishes and random-access imaging with sub-millisecond switching times at the full resolution of the camera.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a performance characteristic.

claim: The RAP system enables capture of long-duration records from different samples in parallel, which is not possible using conventional automated microscopes.
source: This enables the RAP system to capture long-duration records from different samples in parallel, which is not possible using conventional automated microscopes.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage over conventional systems in the abstract.

claim: Conventional multi-sample imaging modalities require movement of the sample to the focal plane of the imaging system.
source: Conventional multi-sample imaging modalities either require movement of the sample to the focal plane of the imaging system (Klimas et al., 2016; Yemini et al., 2013; Kopljar et al., 2017; Hortigon-Vinagre et al., 2018), movement of the imaging system itself (Likitlersuang et al., 2012; Hansen et al., 2010), or use a wide-field approach to capture several samples in one frame (Larsch et al., 2013; Taute et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Conventional multi-sample imaging modalities require movement of the imaging system itself.
source: Conventional multi-sample imaging modalities either require movement of the sample to the focal plane of the imaging system (Klimas et al., 2016; Yemini et al., 2013; Kopljar et al., 2017; Hortigon-Vinagre et al., 2018), movement of the imaging system itself (Likitlersuang et al., 2012; Hansen et al., 2010), or use a wide-field approach to capture several samples in one frame (Larsch et al., 2013; Taute et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Conventional multi-sample imaging modalities use a wide-field approach to capture several samples in one frame.
source: Conventional multi-sample imaging modalities either require movement of the sample to the focal plane of the imaging system (Klimas et al., 2016; Yemini et al., 2013; Kopljar et al., 2017; Hortigon-Vinagre et al., 2018), movement of the imaging system itself (Likitlersuang et al., 2012; Hansen et al., 2010), or use a wide-field approach to capture several samples in one frame (Larsch et al., 2013; Taute et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Schemes that move the sample or the imaging system can be mechanically complex and are inherently slow.
source: Schemes that move the sample or the imaging system can be mechanically complex and are inherently slow, while wide-field imaging systems have poor light collection efficiency and resolution compared to systems that image a single sample at a given time point.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of conventional approaches.

claim: Wide-field imaging systems have poor light collection efficiency and resolution compared to systems that image a single sample at a given time point.
source: Schemes that move the sample or the imaging system can be mechanically complex and are inherently slow, while wide-field imaging systems have poor light collection efficiency and resolution compared to systems that image a single sample at a given time point.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of wide-field approaches.

claim: Current imaging modalities cannot continuously monitor several samples unless they are in the same field of view.
source: An important limitation of current imaging modalities is that they cannot continuously monitor several samples unless they are in the same field of view.
evidence: This is stated as a key limitation that RAP addresses.

claim: Many experiments require continuous long-term records in spatially separated samples.
source: As many experiments require continuous long-term records in spatially separated samples, they cannot benefit from these high-throughput techniques.
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the RAP system.

claim: The RAP system uses a large parabolic reflector and objective lenses positioned at their focal distances above each sample.
source: The random-access parallel (RAP) system uses a large parabolic reflector and objective lenses positioned at their focal distances above each sample.
evidence: This describes the optical configuration of the system.

claim: A fast LED array sequentially illuminates samples to generate images that are captured with a single camera placed at the focal point of the reflector.
source: A fast light-emitting diode (LED) array sequentially illuminates samples to generate images that are captured with a single camera placed at the focal point of the reflector.
evidence: This describes the illumination and detection scheme.

claim: The optical configuration allows each sample to fill a sensor's field of view.
source: This optical configuration allows each sample to fill a sensor's field of view.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the optical design.

claim: LED switch times are very fast.
source: Since each LED illuminates a single sample and LED switch times are very fast, images from spatially separated samples can be captured at rates limited only by the camera's frame rate or the system's ability to store data.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the LEDs used.

claim: Images from spatially separated samples can be captured at rates limited only by the camera's frame rate or the system's ability to store data.
source: Since each LED illuminates a single sample and LED switch times are very fast, images from spatially separated samples can be captured at rates limited only by the camera's frame rate or the system's ability to store data.
evidence: This is stated as a performance characteristic of the system.

claim: RAP enables effectively simultaneous continuous recordings of different samples by switching LEDs at very fast rates.
source: RAP enables effectively simultaneous continuous recordings of different samples by switching LEDs at very fast rates.
evidence: This is stated as a key capability of the system.

claim: The current prototypes use fast machine vision complementary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras.
source: Our current prototypes (Figure 1A) use fast machine vision complementary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras and commercially available LED arrays controlled by Arduino microcontrollers, which can rapidly switch between LEDs at kHz rates.
evidence: This describes the hardware used in the prototypes.

claim: The current prototypes use commercially available LED arrays controlled by Arduino microcontrollers.
source: Our current prototypes (Figure 1A) use fast machine vision complementary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras and commercially available LED arrays controlled by Arduino microcontrollers, which can rapidly switch between LEDs at kHz rates.
evidence: This describes the hardware used in the prototypes.

claim: Arduino microcontrollers can rapidly switch between LEDs at kHz rates.
source: Our current prototypes (Figure 1A) use fast machine vision complementary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras and commercially available LED arrays controlled by Arduino microcontrollers, which can rapidly switch between LEDs at kHz rates.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of the control system.

claim: A single-element plano-convex lens is placed above each sample, so that collimated light is projected to a 100 mm focal length parabolic reflector.
source: A single-element plano-convex lens is placed above each sample, so that collimated light is projected to a 100 mm focal length parabolic reflector, which then creates an image on the detector.
evidence: This describes the optical path in the system.

claim: The parabolic reflector creates an image on the detector.
source: A single-element plano-convex lens is placed above each sample, so that collimated light is projected to a 100 mm focal length parabolic reflector, which then creates an image on the detector.
evidence: This describes the image formation process.

claim: The bright-field nature of the illumination allows images to be captured with sub-millisecond exposure times.
source: The bright-field nature of the illumination used in this design allows images to be captured with sub-millisecond exposure times.
evidence: This is stated as a feature of the illumination scheme.

claim: The camera is synchronized with the LED array via a TTL signal from the microcontroller.
source: The camera is synchronized with the LED array via a transistor–transistor logic (TTL) signal from the microcontroller, so that a single frame is captured when any LED is on.
evidence: This describes the synchronization mechanism.

claim: A single frame is captured when any LED is on.
source: The camera is synchronized with the LED array via a transistor–transistor logic (TTL) signal from the microcontroller, so that a single frame is captured when any LED is on.
evidence: This describes the image capture timing.

claim: The setup can rapidly switch to image any dish under the parabolic reflector without moving the sample or camera.
source: This setup can rapidly switch to image any dish under the parabolic reflector without moving the sample or camera.
evidence: This is stated as a key feature of the system.

claim: The system can acquire data from several dishes near-simultaneously by trading-off the number of samples for frame rate.
source: In addition, the system can acquire data from several dishes near-simultaneously by trading-off the number of samples for frame rate: for example, if a 500 fps camera is used, 50 dishes can be captured at 10 fps, or any two dishes can be recorded at 250 fps (Figure 1B).
evidence: This describes the trade-off between number of samples and frame rate.

claim: If a 500 fps camera is used, 50 dishes can be captured at 10 fps.
source: In addition, the system can acquire data from several dishes near-simultaneously by trading-off the number of samples for frame rate: for example, if a 500 fps camera is used, 50 dishes can be captured at 10 fps, or any two dishes can be recorded at 250 fps (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is given as an example of the frame rate trade-off.

claim: If a 500 fps camera is used, any two dishes can be recorded at 250 fps.
source: In addition, the system can acquire data from several dishes near-simultaneously by trading-off the number of samples for frame rate: for example, if a 500 fps camera is used, 50 dishes can be captured at 10 fps, or any two dishes can be recorded at 250 fps (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is given as an example of the frame rate trade-off.

claim: The high NA and large field of view offered by parabolic mirrors have made them attractive to imaging applications beyond astronomy.
source: The high NA and large field of view offered by parabolic mirrors have made them very attractive to imaging applications beyond the field of astronomy.
evidence: This is stated as background on parabolic mirrors.

claim: Parabolic mirrors introduce off-axis aberrations, which corrupt any widefield image formed.
source: However, parabolic mirrors introduce off-axis aberrations, which corrupt any widefield image formed (Rumsey, 1971; Wynne, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Off-axis aberrations in parabolic mirrors have resulted in compromises such as restricting imaging to the focal region and then stage scanning the sample.
source: This has resulted in compromises, such as restricting imaging to the focal region and then stage scanning the sample (Lieb and Meixner, 2001), which have limited its use to niche applications.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: In the RAP design, transillumination from LEDs far from the sample and collimation from the objective lens results in mostly collimated light being refocused by the parabolic mirror, avoiding the introduction of significant aberrations.
source: In our design, transillumination from LEDs far from the sample and collimation from the objective lens results in mostly collimated light being refocused by the parabolic mirror, avoiding the introduction of significant aberrations.
evidence: This explains how the RAP design mitigates aberrations.

claim: The illumination of the sample by a partially spatially coherent source produces greyscale images.
source: The illumination of the sample by a partially spatially coherent source (Deng and Chu, 2017) produces greyscale images, and in our studies, it is the change in this intensity that is of interest.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support the claim about the illumination source.

claim: Propagation-based phase contrast in the RAP imaging system is generated when collimated light from the LED is diffracted by the sample.
source: Propagation-based phase contrast in our imaging system is generated when collimated light from the LED is diffracted by the sample.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of phase contrast generation.

claim: Light that remains in the collection cone of the objective lens is refocused on the sensor by the parabolic reflector at an oblique angle.
source: Light that remains in the collection cone of the objective lens is then refocused on the sensor by the parabolic reflector at an oblique angle (Figure 1C).
evidence: This describes the optical path with reference to a figure.

claim: As a result of the oblique angle, the image moves through focus from one side of the detector plane to the other.
source: As a result of this angle, the image moves through focus from one side of the detector plane to the other.
evidence: This describes an optical effect of the oblique angle.

claim: The region over which the image is in focus is determined by the depth of focus of the parabolic mirror.
source: The region over which the image is in focus is determined by the depth of focus of the parabolic mirror.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the optical system.

claim: Images are subject to a stretch due to the image meeting the camera plane obliquely.
source: Images are subject to two transformations: (1) a stretch due to the image meeting the camera plane obliquely and (2) a small variation in magnification as a function of the separation between the optical axes of the objective lens and the parabolic reflector.
evidence: This describes one of the image transformations.

claim: Images are subject to a small variation in magnification as a function of the separation between the optical axes of the objective lens and the parabolic reflector.
source: Images are subject to two transformations: (1) a stretch due to the image meeting the camera plane obliquely and (2) a small variation in magnification as a function of the separation between the optical axes of the objective lens and the parabolic reflector.
evidence: This describes the second image transformation.

claim: Image transformations can be compensated by post-processing the captured images using equations derived from geometric optics.
source: These image transformations can be compensated by post-processing the captured images using equations derived from geometric optics as described below.
evidence: This is stated as a method for correcting image distortions.

claim: Cultured cardiac monolayer preparations are used to study arrhythmogenesis in controlled settings.
source: Cultured cardiac monolayer preparations (Tung and Zhang, 2006; Shaheen et al., 2017) are used to study arrhythmogenesis in controlled settings and are subject to intense research due to their potential for screening compounds for personalized medicine.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cultured cardiac monolayer preparations are subject to intense research due to their potential for screening compounds for personalized medicine.
source: Cultured cardiac monolayer preparations (Tung and Zhang, 2006; Shaheen et al., 2017) are used to study arrhythmogenesis in controlled settings and are subject to intense research due to their potential for screening compounds for personalized medicine.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: C. elegans are used as model organisms to study the genetics of aging and biological clocks.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans are used as model organisms to study the genetics of aging and biological clocks (Hekimi and Guarente, 2003) and, due to highly conserved neurological pathways between mammals and invertebrates, are now used for neuroprotective compound screening (Larsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: C. elegans are used for neuroprotective compound screening due to highly conserved neurological pathways between mammals and invertebrates.
source: Caenorhabditis elegans are used as model organisms to study the genetics of aging and biological clocks (Hekimi and Guarente, 2003) and, due to highly conserved neurological pathways between mammals and invertebrates, are now used for neuroprotective compound screening (Larsch et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both cardiac monolayer and C. elegans model systems are ideally imaged continuously over long periods to capture dynamics.
source: Both model systems are ideally imaged continuously over long periods to capture dynamics (Larsch et al., 2013; Kucera et al., 2000), which is not possible in automated microscopy platforms that move samples or the optical path.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Continuous long-term imaging of cardiac monolayer and C. elegans is not possible in automated microscopy platforms that move samples or the optical path.
source: Both model systems are ideally imaged continuously over long periods to capture dynamics (Larsch et al., 2013; Kucera et al., 2000), which is not possible in automated microscopy platforms that move samples or the optical path.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of automated microscopy.

claim: Four cardiac monolayer preparations in four separate petri dishes were imaged in parallel at 40 fps/dish.
source: Figure 2A shows recordings from four dishes imaged in parallel containing monolayer cultures of neonatal cardiac cells at 40 fps per dish.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Motion in cardiac monolayers is tracked by measuring the absolute value of intensity changes for each pixel over a six-frame window.
source: Here, motion is tracked by measuring the absolute value of intensity changes for each pixel over a six-frame window (Burton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to the method.

claim: Intensity vs time plots highlight different temporal dynamics in each cardiac preparation.
source: Intensity vs time plots (Figure 2B) highlight different temporal dynamics in each preparation, and an activation map from one of the dishes shows conduction velocity and wave direction data (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An activation map from one of the cardiac dishes shows conduction velocity and wave direction data.
source: Intensity vs time plots (Figure 2B) highlight different temporal dynamics in each preparation, and an activation map from one of the dishes shows conduction velocity and wave direction data (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C. elegans were imaged at 15 fps for four dishes over a period of 5 min.
source: C. elegans can similarly be imaged, here at 15 fps for four dishes over a period of 5 min (Figure 2D–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2D-F.

claim: C. elegans motion paths can be extracted from each image series using open-source software packages.
source: C. elegans motion paths (Figure 2D), which are often used to quantify worm behaviour, can be extracted from each image series using open-source software packages.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 2D.

claim: The RAP system was validated by measuring motion in C. elegans mitochondrial mutant nuo-6(qm200).
source: We validate the potential for RAP to be used in a higher-throughput imaging application by measuring motion in C. elegans mitochondrial mutant nuo-6(qm200) (Yang and Hekimi, 2010), which have a slower swimming rate (frequency of thrashing) than that of the wild-type C. elegans.
evidence: This is stated as a validation experiment.

claim: C. elegans mitochondrial mutant nuo-6(qm200) have a slower swimming rate than wild-type C. elegans.
source: We validate the potential for RAP to be used in a higher-throughput imaging application by measuring motion in C. elegans mitochondrial mutant nuo-6(qm200) (Yang and Hekimi, 2010), which have a slower swimming rate (frequency of thrashing) than that of the wild-type C. elegans.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Mutant and wild-type C. elegans were loaded into a 96-well plate containing liquid media and imaged using an array of 76 6 mm diameter, 72 mm focal length lenses.
source: Mutant and wild-type C. elegans were loaded into a 96-well plate containing liquid media and imaged by using an array of 76 6 mm diameter, 72 mm focal length lenses positioned above each well (see Materials and methods: Configuration 2).
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: Motion was quantified by measuring the fraction of pixels per frame that display a change in intensity of over 25% for 100 sequential frames captured at 15 fps/well.
source: Instead of measuring thrashing frequency directly, motion was quantified by measuring the fraction of pixels per frame that display a change in intensity of over 25% for 100 sequential frames captured at 15 fps/well (see Materials and methods: Image processing).
evidence: This describes the motion quantification method.

claim: The frame rate of the camera is limited to 120 fps in the C. elegans experiment.
source: In this experiment, the frame rate of the camera is limited to 120 fps (see Materials and methods: Practical considerations and Video 1), allowing us to image eight wells in parallel at 15 fps/well.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the experimental setup.

claim: The system allows imaging of eight wells in parallel at 15 fps/well.
source: In this experiment, the frame rate of the camera is limited to 120 fps (see Materials and methods: Practical considerations and Video 1), allowing us to image eight wells in parallel at 15 fps/well.
evidence: This is calculated from the camera frame rate.

claim: The system quantified decreased activity in nuo-6(qm200), which is consistent with published results.
source: The system quantified decreased activity in nuo-6(qm200), which is consistent with published results (Yang and Hekimi, 2010; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B and supported by a citation.

claim: The time needed to perform the 96-well plate assay is just over 1 min.
source: The time needed to perform this assay is just over 1 min (8000 frames/120 fps = 67 s).
evidence: This is calculated from the number of frames and frame rate.

claim: A limitation of the current RAP implementations is that focusing individual wells is impractical when there are more than a few active samples.
source: A limitation of our current implementations of RAP is that focusing individual wells is impractical when there are more than few (i.e. four as in Figure 2) active samples.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the system.

claim: For System 2 (76 wells), the objective lenses had a depth of focus of 1 mm.
source: For System 2 (76 wells), the objective lenses had a depth of focus of 1 mm, which is sufficient tolerance to accommodate most of the wells imaged.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the lenses used.

claim: Images are noticeably blurred in about half of the wells in the 76-well experiment.
source: While we were able to resolve C. elegans and measure activity in all wells, images are noticeably blurred in about half of the wells, and in some cases, some objects in a single well are better focused than others.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiment.

claim: The focal plane can be shifted by changing the LED colour, as single-element lenses show variations in focal length as a function of wavelength.
source: This situation can be mitigated by changing the LED colour, as the single-element lenses used in our system show variations in focal length as a function of wavelength (Figure 3C and Video 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 3C and Video 2.

claim: Optical simulations using ray tracing software confirm that the focal plane can be shifted by 0.981 μm by switching LED colour from red to blue.
source: Optical simulations using ray tracing software Configuration 2 confirm that the focal plane can be shifted by 0.981 μm by switching LED colour from red to blue (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is stated as a result from optical simulations.

claim: Rapid colour switching may be used to increase data set quality at the expense of decreasing the framerate per well or the number of wells that can be imaged in parallel.
source: Rapid colour switching (i.e. alternating image capture between red and blue LEDs) may be used to increase data set quality at the expense of decreasing the framerate per well (as was done in Figure 3—figure supplement 1) or the number of wells that can be imaged in parallel, as twice the number of images per well are required.
evidence: This is stated as a potential strategy with a trade-off.

claim: The push to develop new high-throughput screening modalities has resulted in several innovative approaches.
source: The push to develop new high-throughput screening modalities (Abraham et al., 2004; Oheim, 2007) has resulted in several innovative approaches, ranging from the use of flatbed scanners for slowly varying preparations (Stroustrup et al., 2013), to wide-field methods that incorporate computational image reconstruction (Taute et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2013), to 'on-chip' imaging systems that plate samples directly on a sensor (Zheng et al., 2011; Göröcs and Ozcan, 2013; Cui et al., 2008; Greenbaum et al., 2012; Greenbaum et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Methods that accommodate a biologists' typical workflow depend on automation of conventional microscopes.
source: Despite these advances, methods that accommodate a biologists' typical workflow – for example comparing multiple experimental samples plated in different petri dishes – depend on automation of conventional microscopes.
evidence: This is stated as a current limitation in the field.

claim: Automated microscopes excel at applications where data can be acquired from samples sequentially as a single high-NA objective is used.
source: Automated microscopes excel at applications where data can be acquired from samples sequentially as a single high-numerical-aperture (NA) objective is used.
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of automated microscopes.

claim: A RAP system could be built using high-NA, high-magnification optics.
source: While a RAP system could be built using high-NA, high-magnification optics, this likely would require that each objective lens is independently actuatable in order to achieve focus which poses practical limits on the number of imaged wells.
evidence: This is stated as a possibility with practical limitations.

claim: RAP systems can be used to speed up conventional imaging tasks in low-magnification settings by capturing data from different samples in parallel.
source: RAP systems can be used to speed up conventional imaging tasks in low-magnification settings by capturing data from different samples in parallel (as was done in Figure 3).
evidence: This is stated as a potential application with reference to Figure 3.

claim: RAP systems are better suited for dynamic experiments where multiple continuous long-duration recordings are the primary requirement.
source: RAP systems are better suited for dynamic experiments where multiple continuous long-duration recordings are the primary requirement.
evidence: This is stated as the primary use case for RAP.

claim: Rhythms in cultured cardiac tissue evolve over hours or even days.
source: For example, rhythms in cultured cardiac tissue evolve over hours (Kim et al., 2009) or even days (Woo et al., 2008; Burridge et al., 2016), but display fast transitions between states (e.g. initiation or termination of re-entry Bub et al., 1998), necessitating continuous measurement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cultured cardiac tissue displays fast transitions between states, necessitating continuous measurement.
source: For example, rhythms in cultured cardiac tissue evolve over hours (Kim et al., 2009) or even days (Woo et al., 2008; Burridge et al., 2016), but display fast transitions between states (e.g. initiation or termination of re-entry Bub et al., 1998), necessitating continuous measurement.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Moving between samples in cardiac tissue experiments would result in missed data.
source: In these experiments, moving between samples would result in missed data.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of conventional approaches for cardiac imaging.

claim: RAP overcomes the constraint of missed data by reducing transit times between samples to less than a millisecond without the use of automation or relying on a widefield imaging approach.
source: RAP overcomes these constraints by reducing transit times between samples to less than a millisecond without the use of automation or relying on a widefield imaging approach, while allowing for an optimized field of view.
evidence: This is stated as a key advantage of RAP.

claim: The NA of Configuration 2 is 0.04.
source: Edmund Optics 6 mm diameter, 72 mm focal length (NA = 0.04)
evidence: This is stated in Table 1.

claim: The NA of Configuration 1 is 0.124.
source: Edmund Optics 25 mm diameter, 100 mm focal length (NA = 0.124)
evidence: This is stated in Table 1.

claim: Conventional bright-field 1× microscope objective lenses have NAs close to that of Configuration 2.
source: Conventional bright-field 1× microscope objective lenses have NAs close to that of Configuration 2 (e.g. the Zeiss 1× Plan Neofluar commercial objective has an NA of 0.025, and the Thorlabs TL1X-SAP 1× objective has an NA of 0.03), and research stereo macroscopes have NAs close to that of Configuration 1 (e.g. the NA is 0.11 for an Olympus SZX10 at 1×), but can be higher in specialized macroscope systems.
evidence: This is stated with examples from commercial systems.

claim: Research stereo macroscopes have NAs close to that of Configuration 1.
source: Conventional bright-field 1× microscope objective lenses have NAs close to that of Configuration 2 (e.g. the Zeiss 1× Plan Neofluar commercial objective has an NA of 0.025, and the Thorlabs TL1X-SAP 1× objective has an NA of 0.03), and research stereo macroscopes have NAs close to that of Configuration 1 (e.g. the NA is 0.11 for an Olympus SZX10 at 1×), but can be higher in specialized macroscope systems.
evidence: This is stated with an example from a commercial system.

claim: A high-magnification RAP system would likely require a mechanism for finely adjusting objective heights to keep each sample in focus.
source: As is the case with conventional microscope designs, a high-magnification RAP system would likely require a mechanism for finely adjusting objective heights to keep each sample in focus, as the depth of field of the objective lenses would be reduced.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for high-magnification RAP systems.

claim: The resolution of a RAP system is similar to conventional microscopes.
source: While the resolution of a RAP system is similar to conventional microscopes, RAP systems differ from conventional microscopes in several respects.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to conventional microscopes.

claim: Configuration 1 costs approximately $1750.
source: The cost for the RAP system depends on the number of objective lenses used: Configuration 1 costs approximately $1750, while Configuration 2 (with 76 wells) costs approximately $3,250, as the cost for the cameras in both configurations are similar (~$400).
evidence: This is stated in Table 2 footnote.

claim: Configuration 2 (with 76 wells) costs approximately $3,250.
source: The cost for the RAP system depends on the number of objective lenses used: Configuration 1 costs approximately $1750, while Configuration 2 (with 76 wells) costs approximately $3,250, as the cost for the cameras in both configurations are similar (~$400).
evidence: This is stated in Table 2 footnote.

claim: Wild-type C. elegans were maintained in standard 35 mm petri dishes in 5–8 mm of agar seeded with E. coli for the data in Figure 2.
source: Wild-type C. elegans were maintained in standard 35 mm petri dishes in 5–8 mm of agar seeded with E. coli for the data in Figure 2.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method.

claim: For Figure 3, the mitochondrial mutant nuo-6(qm200) was used along with wild-type C. elegans.
source: For Figure 3, the mitochondrial mutant nuo-6(qm200) (Yang and Hekimi, 2010) was used along with wild-type C. elegans.
evidence: This describes the samples used in Figure 3.

claim: C. elegans were transferred to 96-well plates by washing adults off NGM plates in M9 buffer.
source: Here, C. elegans were transferred to 96-well plates by washing adults off NGM plates in M9 buffer, washed once to remove E. coli, and resuspended in fresh M9 buffer.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation protocol.

claim: All experiments involving C. elegans were imaged at room temperature.
source: All experiments involving C. elegans were imaged at room temperature.
evidence: This describes the imaging conditions.

claim: Cardiac monolayer cultures were prepared from ventricular cells isolated from 7 day old chick embryos.
source: Cardiac monolayer cultures were prepared from ventricular cells isolated from 7 day old chick embryos: cells were plated within 1 cm glass rings in 35 mm petri dishes as described in Bub et al., 1998.
evidence: This describes the sample preparation method with a citation.

claim: Cardiac monolayers were imaged in a stage top incubator at 36°C and at 5% CO2 in maintenance media.
source: Cardiac monolayers were imaged in a stage top incubator (Okolabs) at 36°C and at 5% CO2 in maintenance media.
evidence: This describes the imaging conditions.

claim: A parabolic reflector (220 mm diameter, 100 mm focal length) was mounted 300 mm above a breadboard.
source: A parabolic reflector (220 mm diameter, 100 mm focal length, Edmund Optics) was mounted 300 mm above a breadboard.
evidence: This describes the optical setup.

claim: The camera sensor and electronics were positioned at the focal point of the parabola.
source: The camera sensor and electronics (acA640-750um for data collection in Figure 2, acA1300-200um for data collection in Figure 3, Basler AG) were mounted in a PLA (polylactic acid) housing without a c-mount thread to allow image formation from light at oblique angles and positioned at the focal point of the parabola.
evidence: This describes the camera positioning.

claim: Biological samples were positioned 50 mm above a LED array.
source: Biological samples were positioned 50 mm above a LED array (DotStar 8 × 32 LED matrix for Figure 2 or two NeoPixel 40 LED Shields for Figure 3, Adafruit Industries).
evidence: This describes the sample positioning.

claim: The LED array was controlled by an ATmega328P microcontroller.
source: The LED array was controlled by an ATmega328P microcontroller (Arduino Uno, Arduino.cc) using the FastLED 3.2 open-source library and custom code (Source code 1 and 2, in conjunction with free Basler Pylon Viewer software) to synchronize the camera with each LED via a TTL trigger pulse.
evidence: This describes the control system.

claim: Captured images shown in Figures 2 and 3 are cropped and rescaled.
source: To offset these effects, captured images shown in Figures 2 and 3 are cropped (480 × 480 pixels for Configuration 1, and 640 × 512 for Configuration 2) and rescaled (so that maximum and minimum pixel intensity values fall between 0 and 255).
evidence: This describes the image processing applied.

claim: Dye-free visualization of cardiac activity is carried out by applying a running background subtraction followed by an absolute value operation on each pixel.
source: Dye-free visualization of cardiac activity (Figure 2B) is carried out by applying a running background subtraction followed by an absolute value operation on each pixel:
evidence: This describes the image processing method.

claim: Intensity vs time plots of averaged pixels in a 20 × 20 pixel region of interest show double spikes corresponding to contraction followed by relaxation.
source: Intensity vs time plots of averaged pixels in a 20 × 20 pixel region of interest show double spikes corresponding to contraction followed by relaxation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Activation maps are generated as previously described by Burton et al., 2015.
source: Activation maps (Figure 2C) are generated as previously described (Burton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the method.

claim: The camera used in Figure 2 was chosen for its high frame rate as cardiac activity requires 40 fps acquisition speeds.
source: The camera used in Figure 2 was chosen for its high frame rate as we were interested in imaging cardiac activity, which in our experience requires 40 fps acquisition speeds.
evidence: This explains the camera choice for cardiac imaging.

claim: The imaging scheme captures data at a maximum rate that depends on the camera as well as the system's ability to save data continuously to disk.
source: The imaging scheme captures data at a maximum rate that depends on the camera as well as the system's ability to save data continuously to disk.
evidence: This describes a limitation of the system.

claim: The system's hard drive is capable of continuously saving to disk at 150 MB/second.
source: Our system's hard drive is capable of continuously saving to disk at 150 MB/second.
evidence: This describes the data storage capability.

claim: The camera used in Configuration 2 has a resolution of 1280 × 1024 pixels, which generates 1.25-MB images.
source: The camera used in Configuration 2 has a resolution of 1280 × 1024 pixels, which generates 1.25-MB images: the 150 MB/second limit therefore imposes a sustained base frame rate of 120 fps (150 MB/second/1.25MB = 120 fps).
evidence: This is stated with a calculation.

claim: C. elegans motion can be adequately quantified when imaging at 15 fps.
source: C. elegans motion can be adequately quantified when imaging at 15 fps, allowing us to image eight wells (120 fps/15 fps) in parallel.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for C. elegans imaging.

claim: A faster hard drive or RAID array would significantly increase throughput.
source: A faster hard drive (e.g. an SSD) or RAID array would significantly increase throughput.
evidence: This is stated as a potential improvement.

claim: RAP has been validated in low-magnification, bright-field settings that have relaxed constraints relative to microscopy applications that may require high magnification with optimized resolution and high light throughput.
source: We note that RAP has been validated in low-magnification, bright-field settings that have relaxed constraints relative to microscopy applications that may require high magnification with optimized resolution and high light throughput (e.g. fluorescence microscopy).
evidence: This describes the scope of validation.

claim: The designs aim to maximize the number of independent samples that can be imaged in parallel.
source: Rather, our designs aim to maximize the number of independent samples that can be imaged in parallel.
evidence: This describes the design goal.

claim: The designs opt to use inexpensive components and minimize the device's footprint.
source: We therefore opt to use inexpensive components and minimize the device's footprint, allowing us to either increase the number of samples captured by a single system or alternatively – as large parabolic reflectors may not be practical in a lab setting – duplicate the system to increase total capacity.
evidence: This describes the design philosophy.

claim: The use of low-magnification optics in the current implementation is not a defining property of RAP.
source: The use of low-magnification optics in our current implementation is not a defining property of RAP, as higher NA, high-magnification optics could be used.
evidence: This clarifies that RAP is not limited to low magnification.

claim: The choice of the objective lenses in the RAP microscope is not limited by the parabolic mirror.
source: In the same way that the objective lens is not limited by the tube lens in a conventional microscope, the choice of the objective lenses in the RAP microscope is not limited by the parabolic mirror.
evidence: This is stated as an analogy to conventional microscopes.

claim: The NA of the implementations described are consistent with other low-magnification systems.
source: The NA (and resolving power) of the implementations described above to demonstrate RAP microscopy are consistent with other low-magnification systems.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to other systems.

claim: To validate the optical model, an opaque grid with a 200 μm pitch was used as a test sample.
source: To validate the optical model of the imaging system (Equations 1 and 2), an opaque grid with a 200 μm pitch (#58607, Edmund Optics) was used as a test sample.
evidence: This describes the validation method.

claim: Rescaling the images by the factor given in Equation 1 recovers the image of the square grid.
source: Rescaling the images by the factor given in Equation 1 recovers the image of the square grid.
evidence: This is stated as a validation result.

claim: To compare the performance of RAP to a conventional on-axis imaging system, the parabolic mirror was replaced by a plano-convex lens with the same 100 mm focal length.
source: To compare the performance of RAP (Configuration 1) to a conventional on-axis imaging system, the parabolic mirror was replaced by a plano-convex lens with the same 100 mm focal length and aligned co-axially with the objective lens and sample.
evidence: This describes the comparison method.

claim: A qualitative comparison of images of a US Air Force chart showed that image resolution degradation in the RAP system is relatively modest for small (<40 mm) axial distances.
source: A qualitative comparison of images of a US Air Force chart showed that image resolution degradation in the RAP system, caused by off-axis aberrations in the parabolic mirror, is relatively modest for small (<40 mm) axial distances (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The intensity contrast was used to infer the lateral extent of the optical PSF by comparison to a computational model.
source: The intensity contrast (the ratio of the darkest region in the gridline to the intensity in the adjacent transmissive region) was used to infer the lateral extent of the optical point spread function (PSF) by comparison to a computational model.
evidence: This describes the analysis method.

claim: Estimated lateral PSF widths varied from 13.4 to 21.6 microns over the full range of axial distances used in the 96-well experiment.
source: Estimated lateral PSF widths varied from 13.4 to 21.6 microns over the full range of axial distances used in the 96-well experiment, with performance falling as a function of axial distance.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis.

claim: Performance falls as a function of axial distance in the 96-well experiment.
source: Estimated lateral PSF widths varied from 13.4 to 21.6 microns over the full range of axial distances used in the 96-well experiment, with performance falling as a function of axial distance.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the data.

claim: The chromatic focal shift observed in the experiments was confirmed using optical simulations.
source: The chromatic focal shift observed in the experiments was confirmed using optical simulations (Zemax OpticStudio 18.1).
evidence: This describes the simulation validation.

claim: For the plano-convex lens used in Configuration 2, the focal shift was found to be 981 μm when switching from a red (622 nm) to blue (469 nm) LED.
source: For the plano-convex lens used in Configuration 2 (Edmund Optics #45–696), this focal shift was found to be 981 μm when switching from a red (622 nm) to blue (469 nm) LED.
evidence: This is stated as a result from optical simulations.

claim: The RAP system was demonstrated by continuously imaging multiple cardiac monolayer and C. elegans preparations.
source: The system is demonstrated by continuously imaging multiple cardiac monolayer and Caenorhabditis elegans preparations.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract.

claim: The RAP system detected significant differences between wild-type and nuo-6(qm200) C. elegans strains (two-tailed t-test p=0.01).
source: This estimate confirms that the imaging system can detect significant differences between the two strains (averages shown by diamond and square symbols, two-tailed t-test p=0.01), which is consistent with published results (Yang and Hekimi, 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with statistical analysis.
